cases.text: How much juice is in a lime?
checks: Gives an approximate kitchen quantity with units; acknowledges size/juiciness variation
cases.raw_text:
On average, one standard lime yields about two tablespoons of fresh juice, which is roughly one fluid ounce. 

===MORE===
A typical Persian lime (the standard grocery store variety) yields:
- Juice: 2 tablespoons (1 fluid ounce, or about 30 ml)
- Zest: approximately 1 teaspoon to 1/2 tablespoon

If you are using smaller Key limes, they usually yield significantly less—about 1 to 2 teaspoons of juice each, meaning you will need 2 to 3 Key limes to get the juice of a single Persian lime.

Tips for getting the most juice:
- Roll the lime firmly against the counter with the palm of your hand before cutting to break down the internal membranes.
- Microwave the lime for 10 to 15 seconds if it was stored in the refrigerator, as room-temperature and warm citrus yields more liquid.
- Use a handheld citrus squeezer or reamer rather than hand-squeezing alone.
cases.spoken: On average, one standard lime yields about two tablespoons of fresh juice, which is roughly one fluid ounce.

cases.text: How should I serve an apple to a one-year-old, according to Solid Starts?
checks: Retrieves and attributes Solid Starts rather than inventing its recommendation
Age-appropriate preparation; does not recommend raw chunks or wedges for a one-year-old
Distinguishes the source's thin raw slices/grated options from soft cooked apple
cases.reference_notes: Checked 2026-09-12: source's 9+ month section permits cooked sections, grated raw apple, thin rounds or half-rounds, with or without skin. Whole apples discussed at 18+ months; wedges at 24+ months with readiness qualifications.
cases.raw_text:
According to Solid Starts, you should serve raw apple sliced paper-thin, cut into thin matchsticks, or grated. You can also continue serving soft, cooked apple slices to reduce choking risk.

===MORE===

Raw apple is one of the most common choking hazards for infants and toddlers because it is hard and breaks off into rigid chunks. 

Solid Starts recommendations for a 12-month-old:
- Paper-thin slices: Cut raw apple into extremely thin rounds, half-rounds, or matchsticks (like thin matchstick fries). The slices should be thin enough that they do not pose an airway blockage if swallowed without chewing.
- Grated: Grate raw apple on a box grater and serve on its own or stirred into yogurt or oatmeal.
- Cooked: Steam, bake, or boil apple wedges until fork-tender. Soft cooked apple halves or slices remain a safe option.

What to avoid:
Do not serve raw apple cut into thick wedges, cubes, or quartered chunks. Solid Starts recommends waiting until around 18 months to try a whole, cored apple, and waiting until at least 2 years old before offering raw quarters or thick wedges.
cases.spoken: According to Solid Starts, you should serve raw apple sliced paper-thin, cut into thin matchsticks, or grated. You can also continue serving soft, cooked apple slices to reduce choking risk.

cases.text: What about with the skin on?
checks: Accurately represents the named source: skin is permitted for the thin raw slices in its 9+ month section
Does not turn skin permission into permission for thick raw pieces
cases.raw_text:
Solid Starts states you can leave the skin on as long as the apple is sliced paper-thin or grated. Babies and toddlers often chew on the flesh and spit the skin out, which is normal and helps develop oral motor skills.

===MORE===

Key details from Solid Starts on serving apple skin at 12 months:

- Thin slices: As long as raw apple slices are cut paper-thin, leaving the skin intact is fine. The skin actually helps keep the delicate slice from falling apart in the toddler's hands.
- Grated: Leaving the skin on when grating raw apple on a box grater is also safe and adds extra fiber.
- Chewing and spitting: Toddlers frequently suck or chew the soft flesh off the slice and spit the skin out. Solid Starts notes this is completely normal, not wasteful—it helps build familiarity with whole fruits and exercises oral motor skills like tongue lateralization.
- Cooked apples: For steamed or baked slices, you can leave the skin on if it is completely soft and peels away easily, though many parents prefer removing it for cooked pieces if it becomes chewy or separates awkwardly in the mouth.

cases.text: Can I substitute baking soda for baking powder in pancakes?
checks: Explains not a direct one-for-one substitution
Baking soda needs acid; baking powder contains an acid component
Avoids prescribing an unconditional replacement ratio without recipe context
cases.raw_text:
Yes, but you cannot use a straight one-to-one swap; you will need to reduce the amount to about one-third and add an acid like buttermilk, lemon juice, or vinegar to activate it. 

===MORE===

Baking powder contains both baking soda and a powdered acid (like cream of tartar). Baking soda is roughly three to four times stronger than baking powder and requires an acidic ingredient to create the carbon dioxide bubbles that make pancakes fluffy.

How to make the substitution:
- For every 1 teaspoon of baking powder called for, use 1/4 to 1/3 teaspoon of baking soda.
- Add an acidic liquid to activate it. If your recipe calls for regular milk, replace it with buttermilk, kefir, or sour cream. 
- Alternatively, add 1/2 teaspoon of lemon juice or white vinegar to regular milk for every 1/4 teaspoon of baking soda used.

If you have cream of tartar in your pantry, you can make homemade baking powder by mixing 1/2 teaspoon of cream of tartar and 1/4 teaspoon of baking soda to replace 1 teaspoon of baking powder.

Cook the batter immediately after mixing, as baking soda begins reacting with acid as soon as liquids are introduced.
cases.spoken: Yes, but you cannot use a straight one-to-one swap; you will need to reduce the amount to about one-third and add an acid like buttermilk, lemon juice, or vinegar to activate it.

cases.text: When I mix blue and red light from an LED strip, I see purple. Are the waveforms collapsing to an average wavelength, the same as a single purple wavelength, or are my eyes seeing purple while red and blue are still emitted separately?
checks: Red and blue spectral components remain; ordinary LED mixing does not average them into a new wavelength
Explains additive color perception through cone responses and brain interpretation
Distinguishes nonspectral purple/magenta from spectral violet
Does not confuse superposition with nonlinear frequency conversion or quantum collapse
cases.raw_text:
The red and blue light waves remain completely separate; they do not merge or average out. Your eyes and brain interpret the simultaneous stimulation of your red and blue photoreceptors as purple.

===MORE===

Light waves obey the principle of superposition, which means when multiple electromagnetic waves overlap in space, they pass through each other without altering their individual wavelengths or frequencies. The LED strip continues emitting distinct photons of red light (around 620 to 750 nanometers) and blue light (around 450 to 495 nanometers).

The perception of purple happens entirely inside your visual system:

1. Photoreceptor activation: Your retina has three types of color-sensing cone cells—short (blue), medium (green), and long (red). The blue light stimulates your S-cones, while the red light stimulates your L-cones.

2. Brain processing: Your visual cortex receives signals from both the blue and red cones at the same time, with little to no signal from the green cones. Because there is no single point on the linear visible spectrum between red and blue (which sit at opposite ends), your brain synthesizes this dual signal into an extra-spectral color perception, often called magenta or purple.

3. Violet vs. purple: A true single wavelength at the far end of the visible spectrum (around 380 to 450 nanometers) is technically violet. Violet can activate S-cones along with a slight secondary sensitivity in L-cones, which is why a single wavelength of violet light looks similar to an optical mix of red and blue light, even though the physical light entering your eye is entirely different.
cases.spoken: The red and blue light waves remain completely separate; they do not merge or average out. Your eyes and brain interpret the simultaneous stimulation of your red and blue photoreceptors as purple.
